The stored charge is proportional to the voltage across it, $Q=CV$, where the **capacitance** $C$ depends only on the geometry and the dielectric. EJU questions test the energy stored, the effect of a dielectric or changed plate gap, and series/parallel combinations — and, importantly, the **Joule heat** dissipated when charge redistributes.

## Key concepts
- **Capacitance** $C$ (電気容量): $C=\dfrac{Q}{V}$, unit farad ($\mathrm F=\mathrm{C/V}$). For a parallel-plate capacitor, $C=\varepsilon\dfrac{S}{d}$ (plate area $S$, gap $d$, permittivity $\varepsilon$).
- **Dielectric** (誘電体): inserting one multiplies $C$ by the relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r>1$, because it reduces the field for the same charge.
- **Stored energy** (静電エネルギー): $U=\tfrac12CV^2=\tfrac12QV=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$ — the work done charging it, stored in the field.
- **Series** (直列): plates share the **same charge** $Q$; voltages add. Combined $\dfrac1C=\sum\dfrac1{C_i}$ (smaller than the smallest).
- **Parallel** (並列): plates share the **same voltage** $V$; charges add. Combined $C=\sum C_i$.
- Which quantity is held fixed matters: a capacitor **connected to a battery** keeps $V$ fixed; a **disconnected** (isolated) capacitor keeps $Q$ fixed. Changing $d$ or inserting a dielectric then changes the other quantities and the stored energy.

## Formulas & key facts
- $Q=CV$; parallel-plate $C=\varepsilon\dfrac{S}{d}=\varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0\dfrac{S}{d}$.
- Energy: $U=\tfrac12CV^2=\tfrac12QV=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$.
- Series: $\dfrac1C=\sum\dfrac1{C_i}$ (same $Q$). Parallel: $C=\sum C_i$ (same $V$).

## How the EJU tests it
The signature item: a charged capacitor $C$ (charge $Q$) and an uncharged one are connected through a resistor by closing a switch; charge redistributes until currents stop. You find the **final charge** by conservation of charge and equal final voltage, and the **Joule heat** in the resistor as the drop in total stored energy, $Q_{\text{heat}}=U_{\text{initial}}-U_{\text{final}}$ — independent of $R$.

## Worked example
Capacitor $C$ holds charge $Q$; capacitor $2C$ is uncharged. Close the switch. Charge is conserved: final total $Q$ over combined parallel capacitance $3C$ gives common voltage $V_f=\dfrac{Q}{3C}$. Initial energy $\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}$; final energy $\dfrac12(3C)V_f^2=\dfrac{Q^2}{6C}$. Joule heat $=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}-\dfrac{Q^2}{6C}=\dfrac{Q^2}{3C}$.

## Common mistakes
- Swapping the series/parallel rules — capacitors are **opposite** to resistors: series shares charge, parallel shares voltage.
- Forgetting energy is lost as heat during charge redistribution even with no explicit resistance shown.
- Mixing up which quantity is fixed (battery connected → $V$ fixed; disconnected → $Q$ fixed) when changing the gap or dielectric.
dc-circuits:
**DC circuits are analysed with Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules; resistors combine in series/parallel, dissipate Joule heat, and real cells have internal resistance.**

## Overview
A direct-current circuit has a steady current driven by a battery through resistors. **Ohm's law** relates voltage, current and resistance; **Kirchhoff's rules** handle any network. You must be able to reduce series/parallel resistor combinations, compute **power** and **Joule heat**, and account for a cell's **internal resistance**. This is one of the most reliable EJU items — usually a comparison of two wirings or a specific branch current.

## Key concepts
- **Ohm's law** (オームの法則): $V=IR$ — the voltage across a resistor equals current times resistance $R$ (抵抗, ohms $\Omega$).
- **Series**: same current; resistances add, $R=\sum R_i$. **Parallel**: same voltage; $\dfrac1R=\sum\dfrac1{R_i}$.
- **Power / consumption** (消費電力): a resistor dissipates $P=VI=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2}{R}$ (watts).
- **Joule heat** (ジュール熱): energy dissipated as heat, $Q=Pt=I^2Rt$ (joules).
- **Kirchhoff's rules** (キルヒホッフ): (1) **junction rule** — total current into a node equals current out (charge conservation); (2) **loop rule** — the sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). Assign current directions and be consistent with signs.
- **Internal resistance** $r$ (内部抵抗): a real cell of emf $\varepsilon$ has terminal voltage $V=\varepsilon-Ir$; some power is lost inside the cell.

## Formulas & key facts
- $V=IR$; power $P=VI=I^2R=\dfrac{V^2}{R}$; Joule heat $Q=I^2Rt$.
- Series $R=\sum R_i$; parallel $\dfrac1R=\sum\dfrac1{R_i}$.
- Real cell: $V_{\text{terminal}}=\varepsilon-Ir$; current in a single loop $I=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{R+r}$.

## How the EJU tests it
A common item wires equal resistors two different ways with an ideal battery and asks for the ratio of **total power** consumed ($P_1/P_2$), or the current through one specific resistor, or the power in an unknown resistor given a branch current. Two-battery networks require Kirchhoff to find a branch current's magnitude and direction. Keep the nice numbers clean.

## Worked example
Three equal resistors $R$ with a battery of emf $V$: wired all in **series**, total $3R$, power $P_1=\dfrac{V^2}{3R}$. Wired all in **parallel**, total $\dfrac{R}{3}$, power $P_2=\dfrac{V^2}{R/3}=\dfrac{3V^2}{R}$. Ratio $\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}=\dfrac{1}{9}$.

## Common mistakes
- Applying series/parallel formulas to the wrong grouping — trace which resistors actually share a current vs a voltage.
- Ignoring internal resistance when the problem states it; terminal voltage is $\varepsilon-Ir$, not $\varepsilon$.
- Sign errors in Kirchhoff loops from inconsistent assumed current directions.
semiconductors:
**Semiconductors conduct via electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type); a p–n junction conducts only in forward bias, acting as a diode.**

## Overview
A **semiconductor** (like silicon) conducts far less than a metal but much more than an insulator, and its conductivity is controlled by adding tiny amounts of impurities (doping). Doping creates **n-type** (extra electrons) or **p-type** (holes) material; joining them makes a **p–n junction**, the basis of the **diode**. On the EJU this is a light, mostly conceptual topic: identify carrier type and the one-way behaviour of a diode.

## Key concepts
- **Intrinsic semiconductor**: pure silicon has few charge carriers; conductivity rises with temperature.
- **n-type** (n型): doped with a **donor** impurity that supplies extra free **electrons** (majority carriers negative). The material stays electrically neutral overall.
- **p-type** (p型): doped with an **acceptor** impurity that creates **holes** (missing electrons) which act as positive majority carriers.
- **p–n junction** (p-n接合): joining p and n material; near the boundary carriers recombine leaving a depletion region and a built-in field.
- **Diode** (ダイオード): a p–n junction that conducts in **forward bias** (p connected to $+$, n to $-$) but blocks in **reverse bias** — a one-way valve used for **rectification** (converting AC to DC).

## Formulas & key facts
- No heavy formula; this is qualitative. Key rule: **current flows through a diode only in the forward direction** (p→n conventional current).
- Majority carriers: n-type → electrons; p-type → holes. Both materials are overall neutral.

## How the EJU tests it
Expect a single conceptual item (block IV or V flavour): identify whether a doped sample is n- or p-type and its majority carrier, state which way a diode is biased to conduct, or pick the correct output of a simple rectifier/diode circuit. Occasionally a statement-selection ("which is correct about semiconductors") format.

## Worked example
A diode is placed in series with a resistor and an AC source. During the half-cycle that makes the p-side positive relative to the n-side, the diode is **forward-biased** and current flows; during the opposite half-cycle it is reverse-biased and blocks. The result is a pulsed one-directional (rectified) current through the resistor.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking n-type material is negatively charged — it is **neutral**; only its *majority carriers* are electrons.
- Reversing the conducting direction of a diode: it passes current from p to n (forward bias), not the reverse.
- Confusing holes (absence of an electron, behaving as $+$) with actual positive ions.
magnetic-field:
**Electric currents create magnetic fields whose magnitude and direction follow the right-hand rule: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ near a straight wire, $\mu_0 n I$ inside a solenoid.**

## Overview
A current is a stream of moving charge, and moving charge produces a **magnetic field** (磁場). The field's strength is measured by the **magnetic flux density** $B$, and its direction is set by the **right-hand rule**. Standard geometries — straight wire, circular loop, solenoid — have simple formulas. EJU items ask for the field magnitude and direction at a point, or where the fields of several wires cancel.

## Key concepts
- **Magnetic field / flux density** $B$ (磁束密度): the vector field around currents, unit tesla ($\mathrm T$). Field lines form closed loops (no magnetic "charges").
- **Straight current** (直線電流): a long straight wire produces circular field lines around it; grasp the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current, and the fingers curl in the field direction. Magnitude $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$, falling off as $1/r$.
- **Circular current** (円電流): a current loop of radius $r$ makes a field $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$ at its centre; the loop acts like a small magnet with poles set by the right-hand rule.
- **Solenoid** (ソレノイド): a long coil with $n$ turns per metre gives an almost uniform field inside, $B=\mu_0 n I$, independent of the radius; outside it is weak.
- Fields from several wires **superpose as vectors** — this is how a "field is zero at point X" question works.

## Formulas & key facts
- Straight wire: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$ (perpendicular distance $r$).
- Circular loop centre: $B=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$.
- Solenoid interior: $B=\mu_0 n I$ ($n$ = turns per unit length).
- $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space (usually given as the symbol $\mu_0$).

## How the EJU tests it
Two or three long parallel wires carry given currents; find the point where the net field is **zero** (a ratio like $d/a$), or the magnitude/direction of the field at a stated point (e.g. a square's corner). Use $B\propto I/r$ for each wire and add as vectors, fixing directions with the right-hand rule. Answers are symbolic ratios.

## Worked example
Wires at $x=-a$ (current $I$, out of page) and $x=a$ (current $2I$, out of page). Between them the fields oppose. Setting magnitudes equal at $x=d$: $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(d+a)}=\dfrac{\mu_0 (2I)}{2\pi(a-d)}$. Cross-multiplying, $a-d=2(d+a)$, giving $d=-\dfrac{a}{3}$ (a point on the weaker-current side).

## Common mistakes
- Using the $1/r^2$ Coulomb dependence — a straight wire's field goes as $1/r$.
- Adding field magnitudes without checking directions; two same-direction currents' fields *oppose* between the wires.
- Confusing the solenoid formula ($\mu_0 n I$, uniform) with the single-loop formula.
magnetic-force:
**A magnetic field exerts a force on currents ($F=BIL$) and on moving charges (Lorentz force $F=qvB$), always perpendicular to the velocity, so charges move in circles.**

## Overview
Magnetic fields push on moving charge. A current-carrying wire in a field feels a force $F=BIL\sin\theta$; a single moving charge feels the **Lorentz force** $F=qvB\sin\theta$. Because this force is always **perpendicular** to the velocity, it changes direction but never speed — bending charged particles into circles. Direction comes from the right-hand (or Fleming's left-hand) rule. EJU items use force balance or circular motion of a particle.

## Key concepts
- **Force on a current** (電流が受ける力): a wire of length $L$ carrying current $I$ at angle $\theta$ to a field $B$ feels $F=BIL\sin\theta$, direction given by the right-hand rule (current × field).
- **Parallel currents** (平行電流): two parallel wires **attract** if their currents are in the same direction, **repel** if opposite — each sits in the other's field. Force per length $\propto\dfrac{I_1 I_2}{r}$.
- **Lorentz force** (ローレンツ力): a charge $q$ moving at speed $v$ across a field feels $F=qvB\sin\theta$, perpendicular to both $\vec v$ and $\vec B$. It does **no work** (⟂ to motion) so speed is constant.
- **Charged particle in a field** (荷電粒子): with $\vec v\perp\vec B$, the Lorentz force is centripetal: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, so the radius is $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$ and the period $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ (independent of speed).
- **Hall effect** (ホール効果): in a current-carrying conductor in a transverse field, charges deflect to one side, creating a measurable transverse voltage that reveals the carrier sign.

## Formulas & key facts
- Force on current: $F=BIL\sin\theta$ (max when $\theta=90^\circ$).
- Lorentz force: $F=qvB\sin\theta$; does no work, so $|v|$ constant.
- Circular motion: $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$, $T=\dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$ (period independent of $v$ and $r$).

## How the EJU tests it
Two setups recur. (1) A current-carrying rod hangs by wires in a field and rests at an angle $\theta$ from vertical; use force balance ($BIL$ horizontal vs $mg$) to express the flux density $B$. (2) A charged particle enters a field region — find where it exits, the landing coordinate/time, or the $r$-vs-$B$ relationship. Answers are symbolic.

## Worked example
A conducting rod (mass $m$, length $L$) hangs from two wires carrying current $I$ in an upward field $B$; it rests at angle $\theta$ from vertical. The horizontal magnetic force $BIL$ balances the horizontal component of the wire tension while gravity $mg$ is vertical: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{BIL}{mg}$, so $B=\dfrac{mg\tan\theta}{IL}$.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking the magnetic force does work — it is perpendicular to $v$, so it changes direction only, not kinetic energy.
- Getting the force direction wrong: use the right-hand rule consistently and remember a **negative** charge reverses it.
- Same-direction parallel currents **attract** (a frequent sign trap).
em-induction:
**A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf (Faraday's law) directed to oppose the change (Lenz's law); a rod moving in a field gives $\varepsilon=BLv$.**

## Overview
**Electromagnetic induction** is the reverse of "current makes field": a *changing* magnetic flux through a loop drives a current. **Faraday's law** gives the size of the induced emf; **Lenz's law** gives its direction — always so as to **oppose** the change that caused it. This is the principle of generators and transformers, and on the EJU it is tested through sliding-rod problems and induced-current-direction questions.

## Key concepts
- **Magnetic flux** $\Phi$: $\Phi=BA$ (field times perpendicular area threaded), unit weber ($\mathrm{Wb}$). Induction responds to how $\Phi$ **changes**, via $B$, $A$, or orientation.
- **Faraday's law** (ファラデーの法則): the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux, $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$ ($N$ turns). Faster change → larger emf.
- **Lenz's law** (レンツの法則): the induced current flows so its own magnetic field **opposes** the change in flux (the minus sign). Increasing flux → induced current opposes it; decreasing flux → induced current tries to maintain it.
- **Induced emf of a moving rod** (誘導起電力): a rod of length $L$ moving at speed $v$ perpendicular to $B$ generates $\varepsilon=BLv$ (motional emf); if it closes a circuit of resistance $R$, current $I=\dfrac{BLv}{R}$ flows and a retarding force $F=BIL$ opposes the motion.
- **Eddy currents** (渦電流): induced loops of current in a solid conductor moving through a field; they dissipate energy and damp motion.
- **Self-induction** (自己誘導): a coil opposes changes in its own current, $\varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. **Mutual induction** (相互誘導): a changing current in one coil induces an emf in a neighbouring coil (the transformer principle).

## Formulas & key facts
- Faraday: $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$, $\Phi=BA$.
- Motional emf: $\varepsilon=BLv$; induced current $I=\dfrac{BLv}{R}$; retarding force $F=BIL=\dfrac{B^2L^2v}{R}$.
- Self-induction: $\varepsilon=-L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$ ($L$ = self-inductance, henry).

## How the EJU tests it
A coil/loop moves near a magnet, or the field through a fixed loop varies with time (given a $B$–$t$ graph); you state the **induced-current direction** (clockwise/counter-clockwise) and the **direction of the force**, using Lenz's and Faraday's laws. Sliding-rod-on-rails items ask for the induced current, the force, or the resulting acceleration/terminal speed. A $B$–$t$ graph maps to a force-vs-time graph.

## Worked example
A square coil moves at speed $v$ **away** from directly below a bar magnet (N pole pointing down). As it recedes, the downward flux through it **decreases**. By Lenz's law the induced current flows to **maintain** that downward flux — clockwise when viewed from above (so the coil's top face acts as an S pole, attracting the descending N pole and opposing separation). The magnetic force on the coil therefore points back **toward** the magnet.

## Common mistakes
- Getting the induced-current direction backwards by forgetting Lenz's law (it *opposes* the change).
- Using the instantaneous $\Phi$ instead of its **rate of change** — no change, no emf, even in a strong field.
- Forgetting that the induced current creates a force opposing the motion (energy comes from whatever moves the rod).
ac-circuits:
**Alternating current varies sinusoidally; its effective (rms) value is peak$/\sqrt2$, inductors and capacitors have frequency-dependent reactance, and EM waves travel at $c=f\lambda$.**

## Overview
An **alternating current** (交流) reverses periodically, $v=V_0\sin\omega t$. To handle average power we use **effective (rms) values**. Inductors and capacitors resist AC through frequency-dependent **reactance**, and an $LC$ circuit **resonates** at a particular frequency. The topic closes with **electromagnetic waves** — self-propagating oscillating fields, of which light is one example. EJU coverage is light and formula-based.

## Key concepts
- **AC** (交流): voltage/current oscillate sinusoidally at angular frequency $\omega=2\pi f$.
- **Effective (rms) value** (実効値): the DC value giving the same average power; $V_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}$, $I_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$. Average power in a resistor $\bar P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}$.
- **Reactance** (リアクタンス): opposition to AC by reactive elements. Inductor: $X_L=\omega L$ (grows with frequency). Capacitor: $X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$ (falls with frequency). A capacitor blocks DC; an inductor passes DC freely.
- **Impedance** (インピーダンス) $Z$: total AC opposition combining $R$ and reactances; for a series $RLC$, $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ and $I_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}}{Z}$.
- **Resonant circuit** (共振回路): a series $LC$ resonates when $X_L=X_C$, i.e. $\omega=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$; then $Z$ is minimum and current is maximum.
- **Electromagnetic wave** (電磁波): oscillating electric and magnetic fields propagating together at speed $c=f\lambda$ (in vacuum $c\approx3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$). The spectrum runs radio → microwave → infrared → visible → UV → X-ray → γ-ray.

## Formulas & key facts
- $V_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}$; average resistor power $\bar P=I_{\text{rms}}^2R=\dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R}$.
- $X_L=\omega L$, $X_C=\dfrac{1}{\omega C}$; resonance $\omega_0=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, $f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.
- EM wave: $c=f\lambda$; $c\approx3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ in vacuum.

## How the EJU tests it
Expect compact items: convert peak to rms (or find average power), compute a reactance or the resonant frequency $f_0=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$, or order regions of the EM spectrum by wavelength/frequency. Occasionally a conceptual point (a capacitor blocks DC, an inductor passes it). Arithmetic stays light with $\sqrt2$ factors.

## Worked example
An AC supply has peak voltage $V_0=100\ \mathrm{V}$ across a resistor $R=50\ \Omega$. The rms voltage is $V_{\text{rms}}=\dfrac{100}{\sqrt2}\approx70.7\ \mathrm{V}$, so the average power is $\bar P=\dfrac{V_{\text{rms}}^2}{R}=\dfrac{(100/\sqrt2)^2}{50}=\dfrac{5000}{50}=100\ \mathrm{W}$ — half the peak-based value $V_0^2/R$.

## Common mistakes
- Using peak values for average power — average power needs **rms** values (the $\sqrt2$ factor).
- Swapping the frequency dependence: $X_L$ *rises* with $f$, $X_C$ *falls*.
- Forgetting a capacitor blocks steady DC while an inductor blocks rapid changes.
atomic-physics:
**Atoms (modern physics) covers the quantum nature of light and matter, the structure and energy levels of atoms, radioactive nuclei, and the elementary particles that build matter.**

## Overview
The Atoms block (V) is short — usually just **one** item per paper — but it is a reliable, formula-light mark. It introduces the quantum world: light comes in **photons** of energy $hf$, matter has a **wave** nature (de Broglie), atoms have discrete **energy levels** (Bohr) producing line spectra, and nuclei **decay** with a fixed half-life. Finally, protons and neutrons are built from **quarks**. Memorizing a handful of relations secures this mark.

## Key concepts
- **Wave–particle duality**: light shows particle behaviour (photoelectric effect, photons) and matter shows wave behaviour (electron diffraction, de Broglie wavelength).
- **Atomic structure**: the **Bohr model** has electrons in discrete energy levels; transitions emit/absorb photons of energy equal to the level difference, giving line spectra.
- **Nuclei**: made of protons and neutrons (**isotopes** differ in neutron number); unstable nuclei undergo α/β/γ **decay** with a characteristic **half-life**; **nuclear reactions** conserve mass number and charge and release energy per $E=mc^2$.
- **Elementary particles**: protons and neutrons are combinations of **up** and **down quarks**; four fundamental forces govern all interactions.

## Formulas & key facts
- Photon energy: $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Photoelectric: $\tfrac12mv_{\max}^2=hf-W$.
- de Broglie: $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{mv}$. Bohr transition: $hf=E_{\text{high}}-E_{\text{low}}$.
- Decay: $N=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$. Mass–energy: $E=mc^2$.

## How the EJU tests it
The single Atoms item balances a fission/decay reaction (counting emitted neutrons via conservation of nucleon number and charge), relates de Broglie wavelength to kinetic energy, identifies a quark's charge, or links photon/electron energy to wavelength. Use the given constants $h$, $c$, $e$; answers are symbolic or small integers.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing the photon relation $E=hf$ with the de Broglie relation $\lambda=h/p$ (energy vs wavelength).
- Forgetting that below the threshold frequency the photoelectric effect gives **no** electrons, whatever the intensity.
electrons-light:
**Light is quantized into photons of energy $hf$ (shown by the photoelectric effect), and matter has a wavelength $\lambda=h/p$ — the two halves of wave–particle duality.**

## Overview
Classical physics treats light as a wave and electrons as particles, but experiments show both have a dual nature. The **photoelectric effect** proves light delivers energy in discrete **photons**; the **de Broglie** hypothesis and electron diffraction prove particles have a **wavelength**. This is the richest Atoms subtopic and a frequent source of the block-V question, so learn the two key equations and the threshold idea.

## Key concepts
- **Cathode rays** (陰極線): streams of electrons from a heated cathode; their deflection in fields showed the electron is a negatively charged particle.
- **Elementary charge** $e$: the fundamental unit of charge, $e\approx1.6\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$; measured in Millikan's oil-drop experiment.
- **Photon** (光子): light energy comes in quanta of energy $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ ($h$ = Planck's constant). Brighter light = **more** photons, not more energetic ones.
- **Photoelectric effect** (光電効果): light on a metal ejects electrons **only** if $f$ exceeds a threshold $f_0$ (set by the metal's **work function** $W=hf_0$), regardless of intensity. The maximum electron KE is $K_{\max}=hf-W$; above threshold, intensity sets the *number* of electrons, not their energy.
- **X-rays** (X線): high-energy photons from rapidly decelerated electrons; there is a minimum wavelength set by the accelerating voltage ($eV=hc/\lambda_{\min}$).
- **Compton effect**: X-ray photons scatter off electrons and lose energy, lengthening their wavelength — direct evidence photons carry momentum $p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda}$.
- **Matter wave / de Broglie wavelength** (ド・ブロイ波長): any particle of momentum $p=mv$ has wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}$; electrons diffract like waves.

## Formulas & key facts
- Photon: $E=hf=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$; photon momentum $p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda}$.
- Photoelectric: $K_{\max}=\tfrac12mv_{\max}^2=hf-W$, threshold $f_0=\dfrac{W}{h}$.
- de Broglie: $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{mv}$; for KE $K$, $p=\sqrt{2mK}$ so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.
- Constants (given): $h$ (Planck), $c$ (light speed), $e$ (elementary charge).

## How the EJU tests it
Typical items express the kinetic energy $K$ in terms of the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ (via $K=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}=\dfrac{h^2}{2m\lambda^2}$), find a photoelectric threshold or max KE, compute a photon energy from wavelength, or reason about how emitted-electron energy/number depends on frequency vs intensity. Answers are symbolic in $h,c,m,\lambda$.

## Worked example
An electron has de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$. Its momentum is $p=\dfrac{h}{\lambda}$, so its kinetic energy is $K=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}=\dfrac{h^2}{2m\lambda^2}$. A shorter wavelength therefore means a faster, higher-energy electron.

## Common mistakes
- Thinking more intense light gives electrons more energy — intensity raises the **number** of electrons; only higher **frequency** raises their energy.
- Below threshold ($f<f_0$), **no** electrons are emitted no matter how bright the light.
- Mixing $E=hf$ (photon energy) with $\lambda=h/p$ (matter wavelength).
atoms-nuclei:
**Atoms have discrete energy levels (Bohr model) that produce line spectra, and unstable nuclei decay with a fixed half-life, converting mass to energy via $E=mc^2$.**

## Overview
This subtopic combines two ideas. First, the **Bohr model**: electrons occupy discrete **energy levels**, and jumps between them emit or absorb photons of exact energies, producing the sharp lines of atomic spectra (e.g. the hydrogen spectrum). Second, the **nucleus**: it is built of protons and neutrons, comes in **isotopes**, and if unstable **decays** with a characteristic **half-life**, releasing energy governed by mass–energy equivalence. Both give clean, high-yield EJU items.

## Key concepts
- **Bohr model** (ボーアモデル) and **energy levels** (エネルギー準位): electrons exist only in discrete orbits with quantized energies $E_n<0$; the lowest ($n=1$) is the ground state. Levels crowd together toward $E=0$ as $n\to\infty$.
- **Hydrogen spectrum** (水素スペクトル): a transition from level $E_{\text{high}}$ to $E_{\text{low}}$ emits a photon with $hf=E_{\text{high}}-E_{\text{low}}$, giving discrete spectral **lines**. Absorption is the reverse.
- **Isotope** (同位体): nuclei of the same element (same proton number $Z$) but different neutron number, hence different mass number $A$.
- **Nuclear decay** (核崩壊): **α decay** emits a helium nucleus ($A$ down by 4, $Z$ by 2); **β decay** emits an electron ($Z$ up by 1, $A$ unchanged); **γ decay** emits a photon (no change in $A,Z$).
- **Half-life** $T_{1/2}$ (半減期): the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay; after $n$ half-lives, a fraction $(1/2)^n$ remains.
- **Nuclear reaction** (核反応) and **fission** (核分裂): reactions conserve **mass number** and **charge**; the small mass difference is released as energy.
- **Mass–energy equivalence** (質量とエネルギーの等価性): $E=mc^2$; a mass defect $\Delta m$ releases energy $\Delta E=\Delta m\,c^2$.

## Formulas & key facts
- Photon from transition: $hf=E_{\text{high}}-E_{\text{low}}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{E_{\text{high}}-E_{\text{low}}}$.
- Decay: remaining $N=N_0\left(\dfrac12\right)^{t/T_{1/2}}$.
- Conservation in reactions: total $A$ (nucleon number) and total $Z$ (charge) unchanged.
- Mass–energy: $E=mc^2$; released energy $\Delta E=\Delta m\,c^2$.

## How the EJU tests it
The block-V item often **balances a reaction**: e.g. U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits into two named nuclei — count the neutrons released by conserving nucleon number and charge. Spectral items use $hf=\Delta E$ to find a wavelength or which transition gives the longest wavelength (smallest $\Delta E$). Half-life items find the fraction/time from $(1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}}$.

## Worked example
$^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U}+^{1}_{0}n\to{}^{140}_{54}\mathrm{Xe}+^{94}_{38}\mathrm{Sr}+x\,^{1}_{0}n$. Conserve nucleon number: $235+1=140+94+x$, so $236=234+x$, giving $x=2$ neutrons. (Charge also balances: $92=54+38$.)

## Common mistakes
- In spectra, using the level energy instead of the **difference** for the emitted photon; larger $\Delta E$ means shorter wavelength.
- Forgetting energy levels are **negative** and bunch up near $n=\infty$.
- Miscounting decay: β decay leaves $A$ unchanged but raises $Z$ by 1; don't change the mass number.
elementary-particles:
**Protons and neutrons are built from up and down quarks, and all interactions are governed by four fundamental forces — the deepest layer of matter, tested lightly on the EJU.**

## Overview
Beneath protons and neutrons lie truly fundamental particles: **quarks** (which build nucleons) and **leptons** (like the electron). Their interactions are mediated by **four fundamental forces**. On the EJU this is a brief, conceptual topic — usually a single item asking for a quark's charge or the composition of a nucleon — so know the basic building blocks without over-investing.

## Key concepts
- **Quark** (クォーク): a fundamental constituent of protons and neutrons. Quarks carry **fractional** electric charge (in units of the elementary charge $e$).
- **Up quark** (アップクォーク): charge $+\dfrac{2}{3}e$.
- **Down quark** (ダウンクォーク): charge $-\dfrac{1}{3}e$.
- **Composition of nucleons**: a **proton** is **uud** (charge $+\tfrac23+\tfrac23-\tfrac13=+1$ in units of $e$); a **neutron** is **udd** (charge $+\tfrac23-\tfrac13-\tfrac13=0$). This is why the proton is $+e$ and the neutron neutral.
- **Elementary particles** (素粒子): particles with no known internal structure — quarks and leptons (e.g. the electron), plus the force-carrying particles.
- **Four fundamental forces** (基本的な力): the **strong** force (binds quarks and holds the nucleus together), the **electromagnetic** force (between charges), the **weak** force (governs β decay), and **gravity** (weakest, but universal and long-range). Strong is strongest, gravity weakest.

## Formulas & key facts
- Up quark charge $+\dfrac{2}{3}e$; down quark charge $-\dfrac{1}{3}e$.
- Proton $=$ uud $=+e$; neutron $=$ udd $=0$.
- Four forces, in decreasing strength (at nuclear scale): strong $>$ electromagnetic $>$ weak $>$ gravity.

## How the EJU tests it
This is essentially recognition. A typical item asks for the charge of a **down quark** in terms of $e$, or which quark combination makes a proton/neutron, or to identify one of the four fundamental forces (e.g. which force is responsible for β decay — the **weak** force). Answers are direct facts; there is little calculation.

## Worked example
Determine the charge of a neutron from its quark content. A neutron is **udd**: one up ($+\tfrac23 e$) and two down ($-\tfrac13 e$ each). Total $=+\dfrac23 e-\dfrac13 e-\dfrac13 e=0$, confirming the neutron is electrically neutral.

## Common mistakes
- Swapping the quark charges: up is $+\tfrac23 e$, down is $-\tfrac13 e$ (not the reverse).
- Assigning the wrong composition — proton is **uud**, neutron is **udd**.
- Confusing which force does what: β decay is the **weak** force; nuclear binding is the **strong** force.
